module_intro: Closes the Intermediate Level with the premise that analysis without risk control is incomplete: position sizing, stop placement, targets, trade management, risk events/news, journaling as a process tool, and common intermediate risk errors.
prerequisites_stated_in_text: Requires Intermediate Modules 1-11 (full narrative/bias construction chain).
module_objectives: Size positions so that a single loss remains a controlled, predefined percentage of equity.
Place stops beyond structural invalidation (origin of displacement, far side of the PD array, or dealing-range extreme) rather than at arbitrary round numbers.
Define targets from the Draw on Liquidity and intermediate liquidity pools rather than from fixed reward multiples alone.
Manage open trades as the narrative evolves (partial profits, break-even, trailing only when structure supports it).
Distinguish trade stop-out from bias invalidation.
Maintain a process-oriented journal that improves bias construction, conditioning adherence and emotional discipline.
Recognise common risk and management errors that undermine otherwise sound ICT analysis.

raw_sections.Fixed Fractional Principle: The intermediate standard is to risk a small, fixed fraction of account equity on any single idea - commonly 0.5 % to 1 % for most developing traders, and rarely more than 1 - 2 % even for experienced ones. The exact percentage is a personal risk-tolerance decision; the discipline of fixing it in advance is not.
raw_sections.Calculation: Position size = (Account equity × Risk fraction) / (Entry price - Stop price), adjusted for contract or lot value. The stop distance is determined by structure first; the size is then adjusted so that the monetary risk equals the chosen fraction.
raw_sections.Intermediate Rule: Never enlarge size because a setup "looks perfect." Narrative quality is already expressed in the decision to take the trade; size remains constant relative to equity.

raw_sections.Structural Stops:
Stops are placed beyond the level that would invalidate the structural premise of the trade:

916. Beyond the origin of the displacement leg that created the PD array or OTE being traded.

917. Beyond the far side of the Order Block, FVG or Breaker that defines the entry zone.

918. Beyond the dealing-range extreme or the liquidity pool that was raided to generate the setup.
raw_sections.What to Avoid:
- Stops at round numbers or fixed pip distances that ignore structure.

- Stops inside the PD array (too tight; normal fluctuation will remove the trade).

- Moving a stop further away after entry because "it might still work."
raw_sections.Relationship to Bias Invalidation: A trade stop-out ends that particular entry. Bias invalidation (Module 11) may retire the entire directional idea. They are related but not identical. A trader can be stopped out of an entry and still retain the higher-timeframe bias if the larger invalidation level has not been breached.

raw_sections.Liquidity-Based Targets: Primary targets are the Draw on Liquidity and the intermediate liquidity pools identified in the bias process. Fixed reward-to-risk multiples (e.g., 1:2, 1:3) are useful as minimum thresholds or partial-profit guides, but they do not replace the actual liquidity objectives.
raw_sections.Partial Profits: A common intermediate practice is to take partial profits at the first meaningful internal liquidity pool and leave a runner toward the external or higher-timeframe Draw on Liquidity. This balances realised gains with participation in larger expansions.
raw_sections.Opposite-Side Liquidity: When the target is itself a liquidity pool, the trader anticipates that price may probe or sweep that pool. Targets may be set just before the pool or managed dynamically once the pool is approached.

raw_sections.Pre-Defined Plan: Before entry the trader states: entry zone, stop level, first target, runner target (if any), and the conditions under which the stop will be moved to break-even or trailed.
raw_sections.Break-Even and Trailing: Moving to break-even is justified when structure has shifted sufficiently that the original risk is no longer required (for example, after a clear continuation displacement). Trailing is justified when a new higher-timeframe or intermediate PD array or structural low/high has formed that can protect the trade. Arbitrary trailing that tightens risk inside normal retracement depth is a common way to be shaken out of good ideas.
raw_sections.Narrative Evolution: If, while the trade is open, higher-timeframe structure or the Draw on Liquidity changes materially, the management plan is updated. The original plan is not sacred; the current narrative is.

raw_sections.Known Events: High-impact scheduled news can produce non-structural spikes that violate otherwise sound stops. Intermediate practice is either to reduce size, widen stops only with a corresponding size reduction, or stand aside around the event window when the narrative does not explicitly depend on the release.
raw_sections.Unscheduled Volatility: When volatility expands beyond the structural assumptions of the setup, the priority is capital preservation. Closing or reducing the position is preferable to hoping the narrative will reassert itself immediately.

raw_sections.What to Record:
A useful intermediate journal captures:

919. Pre-session weekly and daily bias statements (including DOL and invalidation).

920. Conditioning factors required and whether they appeared.

921. Entry, stop, targets, and actual management actions.

922. Outcome (win / loss / breakeven) and monetary result.

923. Whether the bias was confirmed, conditioned correctly, or invalidated.

924. Emotional state and any deviation from the plan.

925. One concrete lesson for the next session.
raw_sections.Process Metrics over P&L: The primary purpose of the journal is to improve the process: bias accuracy, conditioning adherence, stop discipline, target selection, and emotional control. P&L is the lagging result of process quality.
raw_sections.Review Cadence: Daily notes are written at the session close. A weekly review examines the set of daily biases against the weekly bias and identifies recurring errors (for example, entering before conditioning, moving stops, ignoring invalidation).

rules.statement: Fixed fractional position sizing: risk a small, fixed fraction of account equity on any single idea -- commonly 0.5% to 1% for most developing traders, rarely more than 1-2% even for experienced ones. Position size = (Account equity x Risk fraction) / (Entry price - Stop price), adjusted for contract/lot value. Stop distance is determined by structure first; size is then adjusted so monetary risk equals the chosen fraction. Never enlarge size because a setup 'looks perfect' -- narrative quality is already expressed in the decision to take the trade; size remains constant relative to equity.
rules.exceptions_or_qualifiers: Exact percentage is a personal risk-tolerance decision; the discipline of fixing it in advance matters more than the specific number.

rules.statement: Structural stop placement: beyond the origin of the displacement leg that created the PD array or OTE being traded; beyond the far side of the Order Block, FVG or Breaker that defines the entry zone; beyond the dealing-range extreme or the liquidity pool that was raided to generate the setup. Avoid: stops at round numbers or fixed pip distances that ignore structure; stops inside the PD array (too tight -- normal fluctuation removes the trade); moving a stop further away after entry because 'it might still work.' A trade stop-out ends that particular entry; bias invalidation (Module 11) may retire the entire directional idea -- related but not identical; a trader can be stopped out of an entry and still retain the HTF bias if the larger invalidation level has not been breached.

Targets: primary targets are the Draw on Liquidity and intermediate liquidity pools identified in the bias process. Fixed reward-to-risk multiples (e.g. 1:2, 1:3) are useful as minimum thresholds or partial-profit guides but do not replace the actual liquidity objectives. Common practice: take partial profits at the first meaningful internal liquidity pool and leave a runner toward the external/HTF Draw on Liquidity.

Before entry, the trader states: entry zone, stop level, first target, runner target (if any), and the conditions under which the stop will be moved to break-even or trailed. Moving to break-even is justified when structure has shifted sufficiently that the original risk is no longer required (e.g. after a clear continuation displacement). Trailing is justified when a new HTF or intermediate PD array or structural low/high has formed that can protect further gains. If HTF structure or the Draw on Liquidity changes materially while the trade is open, the management plan is updated -- the original plan is not sacred; the current narrative is.

High-impact scheduled news can produce non-structural spikes that violate otherwise sound stops. Practice: reduce size, widen stops only with a corresponding size reduction, or stand aside around the event window when the narrative does not explicitly depend on the release. When volatility expands beyond the structural assumptions of the setup, capital preservation is the priority -- closing or reducing the position is preferable to hoping the narrative reasserts itself immediately.

examples.content:
Bias: Weekly and daily bullish; DOL = buy-side above 1.1000; invalidation = daily close below 1.0820.

Conditioning: Asian low swept, London displacement higher, MSS, FVG in discount.

Entry: 1.0865 (retracement into FVG / OTE).

Stop: 1.0810 (beyond displacement origin and Asian low). Risk = 55 pips. Size set so that 55 pips = 1 % of equity.

Targets: Partial at 1.0920 (internal liquidity); runner toward 1.1000.

Management: After price expands through 1.0920 and forms a new higher low, stop moved to break-even. Runner left until either the DOL is reached or a new daily structural break occurs.

Journal entry records the full sequence, the outcome, and whether every conditioning step was respected.
examples.interpretation_given_in_text: Walks through a complete intermediate trade lifecycle from bias through conditioning, entry, management, and journaling.

book_location.section_heading: Worked Example - Complete Intermediate Trade Lifecycle

relationships.statement: Bias (Module 11) decides direction and the Draw on Liquidity. Conditioning (Modules 3 - 10) decides when entry is permitted. This module decides how much to risk, where the idea is proven wrong, where profits are taken, and how the entire sequence is recorded so that the next bias statement is better than the last. Without this layer the analytical framework remains theoretical.

no_trade_conditions.statement: Common intermediate risk errors to avoid (implicit no-trade/no-action guidance): increasing size after a winning streak or on a 'high-confidence' setup; placing stops inside the PD array or at psychologically comfortable but structurally meaningless levels; moving stops further from entry after the trade is live; taking profits at the first sign of retracement and then watching the Draw on Liquidity print without participation; ignoring bias invalidation and re-entering in the same direction after a structural break; trading with unclear bias because 'the chart looks active'; neglecting the journal until a drawdown forces attention.

key_terms: Fixed fractional risk - risking a constant small percentage of equity per idea.
Structural stop - stop placed beyond the level that invalidates the trade's premise.
Liquidity-based target - objective defined by a pool of resting orders rather than a fixed multiple alone.
Partial profit - realised gain at an intermediate objective while a runner remains.
Bias invalidation vs trade stop-out - retirement of the directional idea versus exit of a single entry.
Process journal - record that emphasises bias, conditioning, adherence and lessons over raw P&L.
module_review_notes.beginner_summary: Beginner teaching introduced basic stop-loss and take-profit ideas. Intermediate teaching anchors stops to structure, targets to liquidity, size to fixed equity fractions, management to the evolving narrative, and journaling to process improvement. The result is a durable operating system rather than a collection of chart patterns.
module_review_notes.concept_relationships_summary: All prior modules supply the analytical content. This module supplies the risk envelope and the feedback loop. Together they form a complete intermediate trading process: narrative -> bias -> conditioning -> entry -> structural risk -> liquidity targets -> management -> journal -> improved narrative.
module_review_notes.practical_chart_exercise:
For the next ten traded ideas (or ten consecutive sessions):

- Before each entry write the full risk frame: equity fraction, stop level and reason, size, first target, runner target, management rules.

- After the trade closes, complete the journal entry including process adherence and one lesson.

- At the end of the ten-idea sample, calculate: percentage of ideas that respected conditioning, average R-multiple, largest deviation from plan, and the single most repeated error.

- Write a one-page revision of your personal risk rules based on that sample.
self_test_questions: Why is position size calculated from the stop distance rather than chosen first?
Give three structural locations at which a stop may legitimately be placed.
How does a liquidity-based target differ from a fixed 1:3 reward-to-risk target?
When is it reasonable to move a stop to break-even?
What is the difference between a trade stop-out and bias invalidation?
What elements of a journal most directly improve future bias construction?
common_misconceptions: "A good setup deserves more size." - False. Size is a function of equity and stop distance, not of narrative enthusiasm.
"I can widen the stop if I reduce size after entry." - Usually a rationalisation; the original structural premise should have determined the stop.
"Journaling is only for losing periods." - False. The journal is most valuable when it captures both adherence and success so that the process can be repeated.
"Once I'm in profit the stop no longer matters." - False. Open risk remains real until the trade is closed or protected by structure.
"Risk management is separate from ICT analysis." - False. Structural stops and liquidity targets are ICT analysis applied to the risk frame.
